explain: Linden et al. build the similar-items table offline (worst case O(N^2 M) for N catalog items and M customers, closer to O(NM) in practice). The online step aggregates neighbours of the user's own items, so it scales independently of catalog size and customer count.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Cold start: content for new items, bandits for new users
question: A new item has rich metadata but zero interactions. Which model can rank it on day one?
options: Matrix factorization with an ID embedding table, retrained nightly
Item-to-item CF using co-purchase cosine
A two-tower model whose item tower reads content features
LinUCB with the item's ID as the only feature
explain: ID-based matrix factorization and co-purchase similarity both need interactions involving the item. An item tower over content features produces a vector from metadata alone, which can be indexed and retrieved immediately.

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: ArUco markers, camera calibration and solvePnP
question: After calibrating a phone camera, the app lets the camera autofocus between shots. Why might measurements drift?
options: Autofocus changes the ArUco dictionary
Autofocus re-orders the detected corners
Refocusing has no effect on geometry, so they should not drift
Refocusing changes the optics, so the calibrated intrinsics and distortion may no longer match
explain: The OpenCV ArUco tutorial says calibration is valid unless the camera optics are modified, giving a change of focus as the example. A homography-only pipeline is less affected because it refits H from the marker in every photo, but undistortion still uses the stored coefficients.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: How the planner chooses: join order search and row estimates
question: A plan estimates `rows=1` for a nested loop's outer input, but EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows 200,000 actual rows and the query is slow. What is the best first fix?
options: Set enable_nestloop = off for the whole server
Raise work_mem so the nested loop fits in memory
Fix the estimate: run ANALYZE, add extended statistics for correlated columns, or add an index
Raise geqo_threshold so more join orders are searched
explain: The nested loop was chosen because of the 1-row estimate; the algorithm is a symptom. Correcting statistics lets the planner cost the alternatives honestly. Disabling nested loops globally hurts the many queries where an index nested loop is best, and work_mem and GEQO do not affect this estimate.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Failures: sloppy quorums, hinted handoff and repair
question: A Cassandra replica was down for 5 hours with default settings, then rejoins. Some writes it missed were never read since. What brings it up to date?
options: Hint replay, since hints are kept until delivered
Nothing ever; the data is lost on that replica forever
Gossip automatically copies all missed rows on rejoin
Anti-entropy repair, because hints stop being generated after the 3 hour window and no reads triggered read repair
explain: Hints are generated only for the first `max_hint_window` (3 hours by default) of downtime. Writes after that are not hinted, and read repair only fixes keys that get read. A Merkle-tree repair (`nodetool repair`) is what restores those keys.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: Goodhart measured: gold reward rises, then falls
question: In Gao et al., a 6B policy and a 1.2B policy are optimized against the same proxy RM. What did they observe about overoptimization?
options: Both peaked at almost the same KL, with a similar proxy-to-gold gap
The 6B policy overoptimized much faster because it is a stronger optimizer
The 6B policy never overoptimized
Only the 1.2B policy reached a peak
explain: Contrary to the intuition that bigger policies exploit RMs faster, gold scores peaked at almost the same KL and the proxy-gold gap was nearly the same. The larger policy did start higher and gained less from optimization.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Assessing risk in practice: from asset list to risk register
question: Risk R-002 was accepted by the CTO until 30 June 2026. It is now November 2026 and nothing changed. What is the correct status?
options: Accepted, because the risk score did not change
Closed, because no incident happened
Transferred to the CTO personally
Unmanaged until someone with authority re-accepts it or treats it, because the acceptance has expired
explain: Acceptances expire on purpose so that someone re-examines the risk as the world changes. An expired acceptance means nobody currently owns the decision, which is exactly what reviewers look for.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Security economics: how much to spend (the Gordon-Loeb model)
question: Which statement is the model's main limitation in practice?
options: It cannot handle money
It needs the breach-probability function S(z, v), which nobody knows precisely for a real organisation
It says security spending is never worth it
It only applies to class III functions
explain: The shape of S is an assumption. The model is a way of thinking about diminishing returns and caps, not a calculator you can feed a real budget into.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: PCI DSS v4: the cardholder data environment and scoping
question: Requirement 3.3.1 says sensitive authentication data must not be stored after authorisation. A developer proposes keeping CVV codes encrypted with a strong key 'for retries'. Allowed?
options: Yes, if encrypted with AES-256
No: SAD must not be stored after authorisation even if encrypted
Yes, for up to 30 days
Only for SAQ merchants
explain: The requirement explicitly says 'even if encrypted'. Retry flows must use the provider's tokens or stored-credential mechanisms instead.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Breach notification clocks and US disclosure rules
question: Which part of the SEC's SolarWinds case survived the July 2024 motion to dismiss?
options: The internal accounting controls claim
Fraud claims based on the public Security Statement's access control and password claims
Claims based on post-attack press releases
Nothing; the whole case was dismissed in 2024
explain: Judge Engelmayer sustained the Security Statement fraud claims and dismissed the rest. The remaining case was dismissed by stipulation in November 2025.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Accountability: what boards, CISOs and engineers have answered for
question: The OCC's 2020 penalty against Capital One focused mainly on which failure?
options: Using a cloud provider at all
Governance: no effective risk assessment before the cloud migration, internal audit not reporting weaknesses to the audit committee, and a board that did not hold management accountable
Not having a bug bounty programme
Paying the attacker
explain: The consent order's findings were about risk assessment, internal audit and board oversight, the governance roles from lesson 1.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Weight sync: resharding and moving the bytes every step
question: A disaggregated run broadcasts a 70B BF16 model (140 GB) from one trainer rank over a single 400 Gb/s NIC every step. Roughly how long is the transfer at line rate, and what is the cheapest big improvement?
options: 0.35 s; nothing to improve
2.8 s; send disjoint shards from many trainer ranks in parallel so many NICs carry the load
28 s; switch to FP32 to avoid conversions
280 s; checkpoint to shared storage instead
explain: 140 GB at 50 GB/s is 2.8 s. The transfer is limited by one NIC. Sending shards from many trainer ranks in parallel (8 NICs gives 0.35 s), shard-to-shard resharding, or overlapping the sync with generation all help; FP32 doubles the bytes.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: Ceilings, hierarchical rooflines and Nsight Compute
question: Nsight Compute shows a kernel's L1, L2 and DRAM points almost on top of each other, sitting on the DRAM slope. What is the best next step?
options: Switch to Tensor Cores to raise the flat roof
Restructure for reuse (tiling, fusion) so fewer bytes reach DRAM
Nothing: being on the DRAM roof means it is already optimal
Raise the clock frequency to move the ridge point left
explain: Overlapping points mean almost every byte touched in L1 also came from DRAM: no reuse. The kernel is on the DRAM roof at its current intensity, so the way up is to raise intensity by reusing data in shared memory or registers, or by fusing with neighbors. A higher flat roof does nothing for a memory bound kernel.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: MTTR: detect, triage, mitigate, resolve
question: A team reduced detection from 8 minutes to 1 by alerting on every service's CPU, queue depth and pool wait. Their mean time to resolution got worse. What most likely happened?
options: Detection and triage are independent, so this cannot happen
More alerts means more deduplication work in Alertmanager, which delays notification
Cause-based alerts detect faster but page more often and from more places, so the alert storm grew and triage took longer than the detection saved
Alerting on saturation is always wrong
explain: Cause-based alerting trades triage time for detection time, and the trade is often bad: every service that is merely a victim now pages too. The SLO-based pattern is to page on the symptom your users feel and keep the cause-level signals as unpaged context, which is exactly what lesson 1 did with 9 groups and 1 page. Saturation signals are valuable; paging a human on each of them is the problem.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Ties, missing documents and the window size
question: Your fused results flicker between two orders on repeated identical requests. Which fix addresses the most likely cause?
options: Increase k
Normalize scores with min-max before RRF
Add an explicit tie-break (best single rank, then document id) after sorting by RRF score
Switch to CombSUM
explain: Exact RRF ties are frequent (any two documents with the same multiset of ranks). Without an explicit secondary key their order depends on hash or arrival order. Changing k changes which documents tie but does not remove ties.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Pinning: building kernel objects where they will live
question: Which struct field must be declared with `#[pin]` and initialized with `<-`?
options: `count: u64`
`name: &'static CStr`
`state: Mutex<State>`
`buf: KVec<u8>` (the vector's heap buffer may be reallocated)
explain: The `Mutex` wraps a C `struct mutex` that the kernel requires to stay at the address it was initialized at, so it is pinned and built in place with `new_mutex!`. A `KVec` may move its *buffer* on growth, but the KVec struct itself (pointer, length, capacity) can be moved freely.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Dispatch queues: how tasks travel from BPF to a CPU
question: Your enqueue callback calls scx_bpf_dsq_insert_vtime(p, SCX_DSQ_GLOBAL, slice, vtime, flags). What happens?
options: Tasks are kept in vtime order inside the global DSQ
The vtime is ignored and the task is appended FIFO
It is an error: built-in DSQs do not support priority-queue insertion, so you need a custom DSQ
The task is silently moved to the caller CPU's local DSQ
explain: Built-in DSQs (local and global) are FIFO only. The docs and scx_simple's comments say vtime insertion needs a DSQ created with scx_bpf_create_dsq(); invalid use is reported as a scheduler error, which unloads it.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: What security architecture is: where every control sits
question: Which of these belongs in the notes app's trusted computing base?
options: The CSS stylesheet for the login page
The marketing website on a separate host
The identity provider that signs session tokens, and the authorization middleware
Every user's laptop
explain: The TCB is what enforces the policy: if the token signer or the authorization code fails, every access decision is wrong. Stylesheets and a separate marketing site do not enforce anything. Laptops are subjects to be checked, not part of the checker.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Assurance: the Orange Book, Common Criteria and what they prove
question: A vendor says its VPN gateway is "Common Criteria EAL4 certified". What should you check first?
options: Nothing more: EAL4 means it resists skilled attackers
The security target: the TOE boundary, the evaluated configuration and the assumptions about the environment
Whether EAL4 is higher than the competitor's EAL3
Whether the vendor's website uses TLS 1.3
explain: The certificate only means the TOE described in the ST met that ST's requirements at that assurance level. If your deployment uses features outside the TOE or breaks its assumptions, the certificate says nothing about it. A higher EAL is more scrutiny of possibly different claims.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: The trust algorithm: criteria, scores and context
question: An attacker with a stolen HR account reads employee records slowly, 25 a day, during office hours, from the victim's own laptop. Which algorithm design is most likely to catch it?
options: A singular, criteria-based algorithm
A singular, score-based algorithm
A contextual algorithm that also uses other signals such as data destinations
None: zero trust cannot detect insiders at all
explain: Every request is valid alone, so singular designs allow all of them. Even the contextual record count stays normal here; SP 800-207 notes an attacker with valid credentials can still reach what the account may use. Context plus other signals (where the data goes, new behaviour) gives the best chance. It is hard, not impossible.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: SASE, SSE and the cloud edge: SD-WAN, SWG, CASB and FWaaS
question: Security wants to know which unapproved cloud file-sharing services employees use and how much data goes to each. Which component is designed for this?
options: SD-WAN
CASB
A stateful firewall
DNSSEC
explain: Discovery of cloud service use (shadow IT) was the first-generation CASB's main job, and current CASBs add data protection and policy enforcement on those services. SD-WAN routes traffic; a firewall sees addresses and ports, not services and uploads per user; DNSSEC authenticates DNS answers.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Threat, vulnerability, exploit, payload and risk
question: A researcher publishes code that shows a router bug can be triggered, but nobody has used it against anyone. Which word fits that code best?
options: A threat source
A payload already in the wild
A risk
A proof-of-concept exploit
explain: Code that demonstrates a vulnerability can be exploited is a proof of concept (PoC). It is not yet active exploitation: CISA says PoC code and security research do not count as exploitation in the wild. The threat source is a person or group, and risk is an assessment, not code.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Scoring and prioritising: CVSS, KEV and EPSS
question: A vector changes from UI:N to UI:R (a user must click something). With everything else the same, what happens to the base score?
options: It goes up, because users are unreliable
It stays the same, because UI is an impact metric
It drops to 0
It goes down, because the exploitability term shrinks (0.85 becomes 0.62)
explain: UI is an exploitability metric. Required interaction makes the attack harder, so the multiplier falls from 0.85 to 0.62 and the base score drops. Impact is unchanged.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Defence in depth: layers, and why they must be independent
question: Three layers each stop 90% of attacks, independently. What fraction of attacks get through all three?
explain: Each layer lets 10% through, and independence means the fractions multiply: 0.1 x 0.1 x 0.1 = 0.001, which is 0.1%.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: STaR and ReST-EM: sample, keep what is correct, fine-tune
question: Your ReST-EM run uses 64 samples per problem, yet 20% of training problems never get a correct sample. Which change gives the model a training signal on exactly those problems?
options: Train for more epochs on the solutions you already kept
Lower the sampling temperature so solutions are more careful
Continue fine-tuning from the last checkpoint instead of the base model
STaR's rationalization: give the correct answer as a hint and keep rationales that reach it
explain: Problems with no correct sample are invisible to the filter; more training on kept data or lower temperature cannot add them. Rationalization samples from a different distribution, p(r | x, y), which can reach the answer. The cost, covered in lesson 3, is more rationales that reach the right answer for the wrong reasons.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Why exact-match caches miss, and how a semantic cache matches meaning
question: Your exact-match cache lowercases text and collapses whitespace. A user asks "what's github", and later another user asks "can you explain what GitHub is". What happens on the second request?
options: Hit, because normalization makes both lowercase
Hit, because both contain the word github
Miss: the normalized strings differ, so the hash keys differ
It depends on the embedding model
explain: Normalization only removes differences you list explicitly (case, spaces). Different wording gives a different string and a different hash. An embedding model plays no part in an exact-match cache, which is why paraphrases need a semantic cache.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Prompt compression: pruning tokens with a small language model
question: Your requests have a stable 3,000-token system prompt (served from the provider's prompt cache) followed by 30,000 tokens of retrieved documents that change per question. Where should question-aware compression go?
options: On the whole prompt, system prompt included
On the system prompt only, because it is sent on every request
Only on the model's output
On the retrieved documents only, leaving the cached system prompt untouched
explain: The retrieved text is long, mostly irrelevant to any one question, and differs per request anyway, which is what LongLLMLingua targets. Compressing the system prompt per question would change the prefix and lose the 0.1x cache reads while saving little.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Validating outbound URLs in code
question: A developer blocks SSRF by rejecting any URL whose text contains "169.254" or "localhost". Why is this weak?
options: It is too slow for production
It blocks legitimate AWS API calls
Python cannot search strings for dots
A string check misses other spellings of the same address, DNS names that resolve to internal IPs, and redirects; the check must run on the resolved destination
explain: Addresses have many textual forms, any domain can point at an internal IP, and a public URL can redirect inward. OWASP's approach validates the resolved IP and pins the connection to it, on top of an allowlist where possible.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Log4Shell: how logging a string ran code
question: An internal Java reporting service never receives traffic from the internet. Was it at risk from Log4Shell?
options: No: only internet-facing servers could be attacked
Only if it ran on Windows
Only if it used LDAP for logins
Yes, if it logged any data that originally came from outside, such as names or headers passed along by other systems
explain: The trigger is a string being logged, wherever that happens. Data entered on a public site can travel through queues and databases and be logged by an internal Java service later, which is exactly the path Cloudflare described.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: File uploads: names, types, storage and execution
question: Why does OWASP say to apply the size limit after decompression for archives?
options: Compressed files are always safe
Decompression changes the file signature
Archives cannot contain executable files
A small compressed file can expand to an enormous size (a zip bomb) and fill disk or memory when the server unpacks it
explain: Compression ratios can be extreme, so a few kilobytes can become gigabytes. Limit the expanded size, using safe extraction code that counts bytes as it goes.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Compressed FSMs: decoding several tokens in one step
question: Which constraint gives jump-forward decoding the largest saving?
options: A free-text field `[\w\s]{1,500}` with no other structure
A schema with long constant key names and enums whose options differ in their first character
A regex that accepts any digit sequence
Plain decoding with no constraint at all
explain: Savings come from compressed edges: text the grammar fully determines. Long keys and early-diverging enums create long forced runs. Free text and open digit runs leave a real choice at every token, so nothing can be skipped.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Dijkstra's algorithm: settle nodes in order of distance
question: Suppose one arc had weight -5 (say, a modeled time bonus). What breaks?
options: Correctness: a settled node's label might later be beaten through the negative arc
Only performance: the answer stays correct but slower
Nothing, as long as there is no negative cycle
The priority queue cannot store negative keys
explain: The finality argument assumes the rest of any path adds nonnegative length. A negative arc can make a path through a far node cheaper than an already settled label. Label-correcting methods, which may lower a label many times, handle negative weights at higher cost: Bellman-Ford makes up to one round fewer than there are vertices, relaxing every arc in each round, so its time grows with vertices times arcs.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: Sampling: why a 7 Hz wave sampled at 10 Hz looks like 3 Hz
question: You have 1000 Hz sensor data and want 100 Hz. A colleague writes `y = x[::10]`, Python slicing that keeps every 10th sample. What is the problem?
options: Nothing: keeping every 10th sample is exactly what downsampling means
Content between 50 and 500 Hz folds into the 0 to 50 Hz band, because nothing removed it first
The result has the wrong length; it should be `x[::100]`
Slicing shifts the phase by half a sample, which is the only error
explain: Keeping every 10th sample makes the new Nyquist frequency 50 Hz. Anything in the original data between 50 and 500 Hz now aliases into 0 to 50 Hz. Low-pass filter first, or use `scipy.signal.decimate(x, 10)`, which filters then downsamples.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: One instruction, many lanes: SIMD registers and lane counts
question: How many 8-bit integers does one AVX-512 `zmm` register hold, and how many 64-bit doubles?
options: 64 and 8
16 and 2
32 and 4
explain: 512 bits / 8 bits = 64 bytes, and 512 / 64 = 8 doubles. 512 and 64 would be counting bits, not lanes; 16 and 2 is the 128-bit case.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Arm Neon and SVE: fixed width versus length agnostic
question: The same SVE saxpy binary runs with n = 10 on a 128-bit and a 512-bit implementation. How many loop iterations does each run?
options: 3 and 1
10 and 10
3 and 3, because the binary was compiled for 128 bits
2 and 1
explain: With 4 lanes the loop runs at i = 0, 4, 8 (the last with T T F F). With 16 lanes one iteration covers all 10 elements under a 10-true predicate. The lane count is read at run time by incw and svcntw.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Bump allocation: a bounds check and a pointer add
question: A bump pointer sits at offset 13 in a chunk. The next request is 16 bytes with alignment 8. At which offset does the object start, and where does the pointer end up (bumping upwards)?
options: Starts at 13, pointer ends at 29
Starts at 16, pointer ends at 32
Starts at 8, pointer ends at 24
Starts at 16, pointer ends at 29
explain: Round 13 up to a multiple of 8: 13 + 7 = 20, and clearing the low 3 bits (20 AND NOT 7) gives 16. Then add the size: 16 + 16 = 32. The 3 bytes at offsets 13 to 15 are padding.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Placing training and rollout: colocated or separate GPUs
question: You have a fixed 64-GPU budget for a math RLVR run with a synchronous loop and short, similar-length responses. Which placement fits the GLM-4.5 report's guidance?
options: 32 rollout GPUs and 32 training GPUs in separate pools, synchronous
Colocated with --colocate, so all 64 GPUs alternate between rollout and training
Separate pools with fully async rollout and maximal staleness
Rollout-only, with training on CPU
explain: For reasoning tasks the report uses colocated synchronous training with dynamic sampling. A synchronous loop on split pools leaves each half idle while the other works.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Launching and debugging a slime run
question: Generations look like garbage, and you suspect either the FP8 rollout checkpoint or the weight sync. Which first step isolates the inference side cheaply?
options: Run with `--debug-train-only`
Run with `--debug-rollout-only` on a few GPUs to see whether SGLang alone generates coherent text from the checkpoint
Increase `--global-batch-size`
Disable `--colocate`
explain: The debug guide suggests `--debug-rollout-only` with few GPUs to test the quantized checkpoint alone; if it is fine, look at the sync with `--check-weight-update-equal`.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Enrichment: asset, identity and intel context, and where it lies
question: Enrichment says the source IP of a failed-login burst is "malicious (feed-A, last seen 2 years ago)" and geolocates to a mobile carrier. What is the soundest reading?
options: Confirmed attacker; block the IP everywhere
Weak evidence: the intel is old and carrier IPs are shared by many subscribers, so judge the alert on the login pattern itself
Definitely benign, because carrier IPs are always legitimate users
Ignore the alert, since enrichment disagrees with itself
explain: Both enrichment facts are weak: stale reputation, and an address that many unrelated customers share. Blocking it could cut off your own mobile users (collateral damage, in RFC 6269's words). The behaviour in the logs is better evidence than the label.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Cloud key misuse, and what Snowflake customers could see in 2024
question: GuardDuty raises InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS for a web server's role credentials. The source IP is the company's own on-premises VPN gateway, and the web team confirms the server routes outbound traffic through it. What is the right outcome?
options: Benign true positive: document it and add a suppression rule scoped to that finding type and the gateway's IP range
True positive: rotate everything and escalate
False positive: disable GuardDuty
Ignore it; GuardDuty will learn the behaviour anyway
explain: This is the benign case AWS describes, and AWS recommends exactly a two-criteria suppression rule. Letting the model learn it silently is worse: you lose the record of why, and anything later using that same remote address, including a real attacker behind the gateway, would stop producing findings.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Talking to users, owners and leaders during an investigation
question: You suspect an employee is copying customer data to a personal cloud account. Who do you contact first?
options: The employee, to hear their side
Their manager, by email
The incident lead and, through them, HR and legal, keeping the case need-to-know
The whole security team channel
explain: Possible insider cases are sensitive: contacting the employee or a wide channel can tip them off, harm an innocent person, or break legal process. The NCSC advises segregating insider threat work for exactly these reasons.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: The sparse autoencoder: a wide, sparse dictionary for activations
question: Why does Scaling Monosemanticity multiply each latent's activation by its decoder norm inside the sparsity penalty?
options: To make the encoder run faster
So the SAE cannot lower the penalty by shrinking activations while growing decoder columns, which would leave reconstructions unchanged
To force exactly k latents to be active
Because decoder norms equal the language model's loss
explain: Scaling f_i down by c and d_i up by c leaves f_i d_i (and so x-hat) unchanged but cuts a plain L1 penalty by c. Weighting by the decoder norm makes the penalty invariant to that rescaling. A unit-norm constraint on decoder columns achieves the same thing.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Measuring an SAE and steering a model with its features
question: You clamp a latent to a large negative value although the encoder never outputs negatives. What happens to the activation?
options: Nothing; negative clamps are clipped to zero
A negative multiple of the latent's decoder direction is added to x
The latent's decoder direction is deleted
All other latents are set to zero
explain: Scaling Monosemanticity notes that clamping to a negative value simply gives a negative multiple of the feature vector. In their code-error example, negative clamping made the model predict the output the code would have produced without the bug.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Kriging is Gaussian process regression in map coordinates
question: A data scientist fits a GP to sensor data with an RBF kernel plus a white noise kernel. In kriging vocabulary, the white noise variance corresponds to:
options: The range
The sill
The nugget
The Lagrange multiplier
explain: A white noise term adds variance only on the diagonal, exactly like a nugget: semivariance jumps from 0 to the nugget as soon as two points are distinct.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Speculative sampling: guesses that keep the target's distribution
question: Which pair of models has the higher acceptance rate beta for a single position?
options: Both are equal because both drafts put most mass on the first token
explain: beta = sum of min(p, q). First pair: 0.5 + 0.1 = 0.6. Second pair: 0.5 + 0.4 = 0.9. What matters is overlap with the target, not agreeing on the top token.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Whisper: a transformer over 30-second spectrogram windows
question: You pass 12 s of audio to Whisper. What does the encoder process?
options: A 80 x 1200 spectrogram, 600 positions
A 80 x 3000 spectrogram, 1500 positions, with the last 18 s padded with zeros
Three 4 s chunks processed in parallel
The raw 192,000 samples directly
explain: Whisper always feeds the encoder 30 s: the low-level API pads the audio to 480,000 samples, and `transcribe` pads each log-mel window to 3000 frames, so the shape is always 80 x 3000 and the stem always yields 1500 positions. The padded tail is silence, which matters later when we look at hallucinations.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The stack: memory that frees itself when a function returns
question: A function returns `&x`, where `x` is one of its local variables. The caller reads the pointer immediately and gets the right value, but after calling `printf` it reads garbage. Why?
options: The compiler moved x to the heap, and printf freed it
x's frame was released on return; printf's own frame reused those stack bytes
Reading a stack variable from another function always raises SIGSEGV
The red zone is cleared by the kernel on every return
explain: Returning only moves `rsp` back up; the bytes are not erased, so an immediate read may look fine. The next call (here `printf`) pushes its frame into the same addresses and overwrites them. No fault occurs because the memory is still mapped, which is what makes this bug so sneaky. The red zone is never cleared by the kernel.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Steering by adding a vector to the residual stream
question: Why can a vector added only at layer l change the model's next-token prediction?
options: Because the model recomputes all earlier layers after the addition
Because the residual stream is a running sum: later layers read the shifted stream and the unembedding reads its final value
Because the vector is also added to the weights of every later layer
It cannot; the vector must be added at the last layer to matter
explain: Each block adds its output to the stream it reads, so a vector added at layer l stays in the sum. Later attention and MLP layers read it and react to it, and the final stream is what the unembedding decodes. No weights change and earlier layers are not rerun.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Side effects and how to evaluate a steering vector
question: Your refusal-steered model keeps its MMLU score, yet users report rambling, repetitive answers. Which check would have caught this?
options: Raising the coefficient
Measuring loss or KL on ordinary prompts and reading open-ended generations, not just multiple-choice accuracy
Running MMLU with more subjects
Using a single contrast pair instead of many
explain: MMLU in the A/B format reads one token's probability, which can survive while generation quality collapses. CAA saw exactly this: multiple-choice capability held while larger multipliers degraded open-ended text. Loss on ordinary text, KL on unrelated prompts and reading samples catch it.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Online filtering: EMA as a low-pass, Welford for anomaly flags
question: Two parallel tasks each computed Welford state for half of a sensor's readings. Can you get the exact overall variance?
options: No, variance needs all raw values in one place
Yes, by averaging the two variances
Yes, by combining (n, mean, M2) of both halves with a pairwise merge formula
Only if both halves have the same mean
explain: Averaging variances ignores the difference between the two means. Chan, Golub and LeVeque give a merge: M2 = M2a + M2b + delta squared x na x nb / (na + nb), with delta the difference of means. This is what makes mean and variance easy to parallelize across partitions.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Causal masks, cross-attention and multiple heads
question: A bug report: a decoder trains to near-zero loss quickly, but generates garbage at inference. Which bug is most likely?
options: The scale factor uses d_model instead of d_k
The causal mask is missing, so during training each position could read the token it was supposed to predict
The model uses 8 heads instead of 1
The softmax is applied over columns instead of rows
explain: With teacher forcing the whole target is fed in at once. Without the causal mask, position i can attend to position i+1 (its own answer), so training is trivially easy. At inference those future tokens do not exist yet, and the model has never learned to predict without them.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Term-frequency saturation: what k1 controls
question: With k1 = 1.2 and average-length documents, doc P contains a term 2 times and doc Q contains it 20 times. Roughly how much larger is Q's factor than P's?
options: About 1.5 times larger (0.94 vs 0.62)
10 times larger
Exactly the same
About 3 times larger
explain: P: 2/(2+1.2) = 0.625. Q: 20/(21.2) = 0.943. The ratio is about 1.5, not 10. That is saturation: ten times the count gives about one and a half times the weight.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Causal self-attention: each position may only look backward
question: A bug report: the mask was built with `torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T))` instead of `torch.tril(...)`, keeping the `masked_fill(mask == 0, -inf)` line unchanged. What does position 0 attend to now?
options: Only itself, as before
All positions 0 to T-1, including the future
Nothing, so its row is all minus infinity
Only position T-1
explain: triu keeps the upper triangle, so row 0 keeps columns 0 to T-1 and the model sees the whole future from the first position. The last row is the one that keeps just one key, its own. The loss will look great and generation will fail.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Generating text: the sampling loop, temperature and top-k
question: A sampling script uses `logits[logits <= v[:, [-1]]] = -inf` (note `<=`) with top_k = 5. What happens?
options: Nothing changes; < and <= behave the same
The 5th-largest logit (and any ties with it) is also removed, so only 4 tokens survive; with top_k = 1 every logit is masked and softmax returns NaN
Top-k now keeps 6 tokens
Temperature stops having an effect
explain: v[:, [-1]] is the k-th largest logit, the threshold that must survive. With <= it is thrown away too, leaving k - 1 choices, and for k = 1 nothing survives: all minus infinity gives NaN probabilities and multinomial fails.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: how bash really runs your commands
lessonTitle: What happens when you press Enter: lookup, fork, exec, wait
question: A script `setup.sh` contains `cd build` and `export MODE=dev`. You run it as `./setup.sh`, then type `pwd`. What do you see?
options: Your original directory, and MODE is unset in your shell
The build directory, because the script changed into it
The build directory, but MODE is unset because export only affects children
An error, because cd is a builtin and cannot run in a script
explain: `./setup.sh` runs in a child bash process. Its cd and export change only that child, which then exits. To apply them to your current shell you must run the file inside it with `source setup.sh` (or `. setup.sh`).

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: how bash really runs your commands
lessonTitle: Exit statuses and scripts that fail loudly
question: A script has `set -e`. Its line `grep -q TODO notes.txt && echo found` runs when notes.txt has no TODO. What happens?
options: The script exits with status 1 because grep failed
Nothing prints and the script continues with the next line
The script exits with status 127
The echo runs because && ignores failures under -e
explain: grep is not the final command of the `&&` list, so its failure is exempt from -e. The echo is skipped and execution continues. (If this were the last line, the script's own exit status would still be 1.)

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: What the geometry means: cosine, analogies and PMI
question: Your search for words similar to *cheap* returns *expensive* near the top. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Antonyms share most of their contexts (prices, tickets, very), so distributional training places them close
A bug: cosine similarity must be negative for antonyms
The vectors were not normalized before training
Negative sampling inverts antonym vectors
explain: The objective only sees contexts. *Cheap* and *expensive* appear around the same words, so their vectors align. Nothing in SGNS or GloVe pushes antonyms to negative cosine.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Prefill and decode: FLOPs and bytes per generated token
question: Which change most reduces time to first token for a request with a very long prompt?
options: Faster HBM only
More math throughput (or splitting prefill across GPUs), since prefill is compute-bound
A larger decode batch
Lowering the number of output tokens
explain: TTFT is dominated by prefill (plus any queueing), and prefill of many tokens is compute-bound. Output length affects total latency, not TTFT.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Where a program's memory lives: code, heap and stack
question: Why does sumsq copy b into rbx before calling square, instead of leaving it in rsi?
options: Because rsi is reserved for return values
Because square may overwrite rsi freely, while the ABI requires square to preserve rbx
Because rbx is faster than rsi
Because the stack is full
explain: The System V ABI splits registers into caller-saved ones (like rdi, rsi, rax) that any callee may clobber, and callee-saved ones (rbx, rbp, r12 to r15) that a callee must restore before returning. That is also why sumsq itself pushes rbx and r14 first: it is about to use them and must hand them back intact.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: From text predictor to assistant: the three-stage recipe
question: A base model is given the prompt "Write a haiku about rain." Why might it fail to write a haiku?
options: It continues the text as a plausible document, which may be more instructions or a list of prompts rather than an answer
Its weights contain no knowledge of poetry, which only SFT adds
Base models cannot generate text without a reward model
The prompt is too short for the attention mechanism
explain: Pretraining optimizes next-token likelihood on documents. A line like this often appears in lists of writing prompts, so continuing with more prompts is a likely continuation. The knowledge of haiku is already in the base model; SFT and RLHF teach it to respond as an assistant.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: RL with PPO: maximize reward, stay close to the SFT model
question: During RLHF, the mean reward keeps rising while the KL from the SFT model shoots up and samples start repeating odd phrases. Which change most directly addresses this?
options: Raise beta, or stop at an earlier checkpoint
Lower beta so the policy can explore more
Lower the PPO clip range to 0
Remove the value model
explain: Rising reward with exploding KL is the signature of the policy exploiting the reward model. A larger beta makes drift more expensive, and earlier checkpoints have less drift. Lowering beta makes it worse; a clip range of 0 stops learning entirely.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Answering AND queries by merging postings
question: You intersect a 10-entry list with a 1,000,000-entry list using the plain two-pointer merge. Roughly how many steps can it take in the worst case?
options: About 10, because the result has at most 10 documents
About 20, because each short entry costs two comparisons
About 1,000,000, because the pointer may have to walk the long list nearly to its end
About log2(1,000,000) = 20 per entry, because the lists are sorted
explain: The plain merge advances one step at a time, so in the worst case it walks the whole long list: O(x + y). Doing about 20 steps per short entry is what you get only if you add skips or binary search into the long list, which the plain merge does not do.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: From main.c to a running program: the four toolchain stages
question: Your build prints "undefined reference to `area'". `main.c` already has `#include "square.h"`, which declares `area`. What is the most likely fix?
options: Add another #include "square.h" to area.c
Pass area.c (or area.o) to the link command
Compile main.c with -O2 so the call is inlined
Add the -E flag so the macro is expanded
explain: This message comes from the linker: main.o refers to the symbol area but no object file or library on the command line defines it. Headers only declare. -O2 (optimization level 2) cannot help: the compiler can only inline a body it can see, and main.c never sees area.c. The fix is to give the linker the definition, for example `gcc main.c area.c -o app`.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Undefined behavior, and the tools that catch it
question: Which of these operations has fully defined behavior in standard C?
options: int x = INT_MAX; x = x + 1;
unsigned u = UINT_MAX; u = u + 1;
int a[5]; int y = a[5];
free(p); free(p);
explain: Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 2 to the power of the bit width, so u becomes 0. Signed overflow, reading one past the end of an array, and freeing twice are all undefined behavior.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Borrowing: many readers or one writer
question: A colleague says the Vec error is pointless in single-threaded code because no other thread can touch `v`. What is the best reply?
options: They are right; the check only matters with threads
`push` may reallocate and free the old buffer, so `first` could dangle even with one thread
`push` always copies the vector, so `first` becomes stale but still safe to read
explain: Reallocation frees the old block, so the shared reference could point at freed memory: a use after free with no threads involved. `push` only reallocates when length equals capacity, which is exactly why the danger is easy to miss in testing.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: The dot product: one number that measures alignment
question: Two unit vectors have a dot product of 0.5. What is the angle between them?
options: 30 degrees
60 degrees
45 degrees
It depends on their dimension
explain: For unit vectors the dot product equals $\cos\theta$, and the cosine of 60 degrees is 0.5. The formula holds in any dimension, because any two vectors lie in one flat plane (the plane of all their combinations), and the angle is measured inside it.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Loss: turning "fits the data" into one number
question: A classifier gives the correct class probability 0.9 on one example and 0.1 on another. Roughly how do their cross-entropy losses compare?
options: The 0.1 example costs about 22 times more (2.303 vs 0.105)
They are equal, since both are 0.4 away from 0.5
The 0.1 example costs exactly 9 times more
The 0.9 example costs more because it is more confident
explain: Cross-entropy is $-\ln p$: $-\ln 0.9 = 0.105$ and $-\ln 0.1 = 2.303$, a ratio of about 22. The log makes the cost grow without bound as the probability of the right answer goes to 0, which is exactly the confident-wrong case.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Fighting overfitting: validation, weight decay, early stopping
question: With SGD and learning rate 0.1, an L2 term $\lambda\lVert w\rVert^2$ with $\lambda = 0.0005$ shrinks each weight by what factor before the gradient step?
explain: The step is $w \leftarrow (1 - 2\eta\lambda)w - \eta\nabla L$, and $2 \times 0.1 \times 0.0005 = 0.0001$, so the factor is $0.9999$. Note the factor 2 from differentiating $\lambda w^2$; many libraries define the penalty with a $\tfrac{1}{2}$ to cancel it.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Backprop in practice: cost, memory, vanishing gradients
question: A training loop calls `loss.backward()` and `opt.step()` every iteration but never calls `opt.zero_grad()`. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, backward overwrites .grad each time
Each step uses the sum of all gradients so far, so updates grow and point in stale directions
The graph is freed, so the second backward raises an error
Weights stop changing after the first step
explain: PyTorch accumulates into `.grad` (the `+=` rule for forks, applied across calls). Without zeroing, step t applies the sum of gradients from steps 1 to t. The official tutorial calls zero_grad every iteration to avoid this double counting.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Concurrency: race conditions and locks
question: On a single CPU with a non-preemptive scheduler (no timer switches), Thread 2 calls a spin lock held by Thread 1. What happens?
options: Thread 2 acquires the lock after one time slice
Thread 2 spins forever: Thread 1 never gets the CPU back to release the lock
The lock automatically turns into a sleeping lock
Thread 1 releases the lock because spinning causes an interrupt
explain: A spinning thread never gives up the CPU on its own. Without preemption, the holder never runs again, so the lock is never released. OSTEP points out that spin locks need a preemptive scheduler to work correctly on a single processor.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Random variables, expected value and variance
question: X is a die roll and Y = 7 - X (the face on the opposite side). What is Var(X + Y)?
options: Undefined, because X and Y are dependent
explain: X + Y = 7 always, a constant, so its variance is 0. Adding the variances (35/6) would be wrong because X and Y are perfectly negatively correlated, and the covariance term cancels them exactly. Linearity still gives E[X + Y] = 7.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Why loss falls on a straight line in log-log space
question: On log-log axes, a team's loss-versus-parameters points lie on a straight line with slope -0.07. Which statement is correct?
options: Each doubling of N removes the same fraction of the loss
Each doubling of N removes the same absolute amount of loss
Loss will reach zero at a finite model size
The slope says how much data the model needs
explain: A straight line in log-log space is a power law: equal multiplicative steps in N give equal multiplicative changes in L, here $2^{-0.07} \approx 0.95$ per doubling. Absolute drops shrink, the curve never reaches zero, and the slope says nothing about data needs on its own.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Inference cost, overtraining and where scaling laws break
question: Exact-match accuracy on a task jumps from near 0% to 60% between two model sizes, while per-token loss falls smoothly. What is the most careful reading?
options: The larger model suddenly acquired a new capability that scaling laws cannot describe
The metric is nonlinear: smooth per-token gains compound into an all-or-nothing score, so the jump may be partly a metric effect
The loss measurement must be wrong
The smaller model was undertrained, which fully explains the jump
explain: Schaeffer et al. show that discontinuous metrics like exact match can turn smooth improvement into apparent jumps, and continuous metrics make the trend smooth again. That is why Llama 3 forecast accuracy through NLL first. It does not prove no real change ever happens, but the jump alone is not evidence of one.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Why keyword match misses meaning and cross-encoders are too slow
question: You must rank 1,000,000 passages for each incoming query. Which cost profile describes a pure cross-encoder versus a bi-encoder at query time?
options: Both need 1,000,000 forward passes per query; the bi-encoder just uses a smaller model
Cross-encoder: 1,000,000 forward passes per query. Bi-encoder: 1 forward pass for the query plus 1,000,000 vector similarities
Cross-encoder: 1 forward pass per query. Bi-encoder: 1,000,000 forward passes
Both need 1 forward pass, because attention handles all passages at once
explain: The cross-encoder has to read the query together with every passage, so its work scales with the corpus on every query. The bi-encoder encoded the passages offline; online it encodes only the query and then does cheap dot products, which an index can speed up further.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Where dense retrieval fails: hybrid search and re-ranking
question: In RRF with k = 60, document X is ranked 1st by BM25 and absent from the dense list. Document Y is ranked 3rd in both lists. Which ranks higher after fusion?
options: Y, because 2/63 is larger than 1/61
X, because a first place always wins
They tie
It depends on the raw BM25 score of X
explain: X gets 1/61, about 0.0164. Y gets 1/63 + 1/63, about 0.0317. RRF rewards agreement between retrievers, and it never looks at raw scores, so X's BM25 score is irrelevant.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Byte-level BPE: how GPT-2 and its successors tokenize anything
question: The GPT-2 regex has no case-insensitive flag, and its source code carries a comment saying it should have had one. What does that cause for the text I'LL?
options: I'LL is one token
The contraction is not recognised: it splits as I | ' | LL
The regex lowercases it to i'll
It raises an error
explain: The contraction alternatives are lowercase ('ll, 're, ...), so 'LL does not match them. The apostrophe falls into the punctuation alternative and LL into the letters alternative, giving I, ', LL. The cl100k_base pattern wraps the contractions in a case-insensitive group.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Learning rate: the stability limit, warmup, decay and clipping
question: On $f(w) = 5w^2$, which learning rate converges fastest?
explain: Here h = 10, and the factor per step is 1 - 10 lr. At lr = 0.1 the factor is 0, so one step lands exactly at the minimum. 0.05 halves w each step, 0.19 oscillates with factor -0.9, and 0.21 diverges.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: HNSW layers: a skip list made of graphs
question: A teammate sets m_L very high (for example 5) so the hierarchy is taller. What does the HNSW paper say happens when m_L is too large?
options: Recall drops to zero because layer 0 becomes empty
Memory shrinks because fewer links are stored
Neighbors overlap more across layers, so extra layers add little and search gets slower
Nothing changes; m_L only affects build time
explain: The paper explains that larger m_L means more overlap between layers (more nodes repeated on many layers), which hurts performance, while too small m_L increases the number of hops on each layer. That tradeoff is why it picks m_L = 1/ln M, matching a skip list with p = 1/M.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Version ranges and lockfiles: why new code arrives unasked
question: Which statement about lockfiles is correct?
options: A lockfile only records direct dependencies
A lockfile makes ranges in package.json irrelevant for npm update
A lockfile freezes the whole tree and checks each tarball's hash, so new releases only enter when someone deliberately updates it
A lockfile stops a malicious version from ever being installed, even when you update
explain: It pins every node, direct and transitive, and stores an integrity hash. It does not judge whether a version is safe: if you update during an attack, the lockfile faithfully records the bad version.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Protestware: when the legitimate maintainer is the threat
question: Which control would NOT have flagged colors 1.4.1 as suspicious?
options: Verifying the package's registry signature
Waiting seven days before adopting new versions
Noticing a test process stuck at 100 percent CPU
Reading the diff between 1.4.0 and 1.4.1
explain: The signature was valid: the real maintainer published it. Diff review, cooldowns and behaviour monitoring all look at what the code does or how the community reacts, which is where a producer attack shows.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Signing artifacts: from long-lived keys to Sigstore
question: A team verifies container images with cosign but sets `--certificate-identity-regexp='.*'` and `--certificate-oidc-issuer-regexp='.*'`. What does a passing check now prove?
options: Only that someone, anyone, with any OIDC identity signed it and logged the signature
That the image has no vulnerabilities
Nothing, because cosign rejects wildcard flags
That the image was built by the team's release workflow
explain: Wildcards accept every identity, including an attacker's. Sigstore's quickstart uses them only to demonstrate; real policies name the exact signer.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: xz-utils I: two years of patient social engineering
question: Why did the 'Jigar Kumar' and 'Dennis Ens' emails matter to the attack?
options: They hacked Lasse Collin's account
They contained malicious patches
They pressured an overworked maintainer to hand more control to Jia Tan
They reported bugs that Jia Tan then fixed
explain: They wrote complaints about slow progress and urged a new maintainer. Shortly after, Lasse Collin described Jia Tan as practically a co-maintainer and gave commit access.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: The Gaussian loop: unbiased fits that still shrink to a point
question: Which statement about the M = 10 loop is correct?
options: The expected variance falls each generation, so the estimator is biased
The typical variance stays near 1, but the expected variance collapses
The expected variance stays at 1, but the typical (median) run collapses toward 0
Both the expected and typical variance stay near 1
explain: Unbiasedness makes the variance a martingale, so its expectation is 1 forever. The median follows the drift of the log and collapses. A heavy right tail of rare runs keeps the mean at 1.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What happens when your program calls write
question: mmap returns a pointer. The raw syscall can also fail. How does libc tell a valid address from an error in rax?
options: A valid address is never negative, so any value with the top bit set is an error
The kernel sets the carry flag on error
Values from -4095 to -1 (the top 4095 addresses) are reserved for errors; anything else is a result
mmap returns 0 on error
explain: On x86-64 Linux there is no separate error flag (the syscall(2) table lists none). Those top 4095 values lie in the kernel half of the address space, never a user mapping, so glibc treats raw results in that range as negated error codes. A user-space mapping address is a normal positive number, but checking the top bit alone would be wrong in general.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Fan-out: why one server's p99 becomes everyone's problem
question: Why does fan-out make tail latency matter more than median latency for the user?
options: Because the root averages the leaf latencies, and averages are dominated by outliers
Because leaves process requests serially
Because the user waits for the slowest of N responses, so a rare per-leaf event becomes a common per-request event
Because median latency cannot be measured at the root
explain: The root waits for the maximum, not the mean, of the leaf latencies. The probability that the maximum includes a tail event grows as 1 - (1-p)^N.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Why summing job durations overstates experience
question: A candidate has two roles: Jan 2020 to Dec 2022 full-time and Jan 2021 to Dec 2021 part-time (both inclusive). A filter asks for 4+ years of experience. What should happen?
options: Match: 36 + 12 = 48 months is exactly 4 years
No match: the union is 36 months, 3 years
Match, because part-time roles always count double
It cannot be decided without the LLM
explain: The part-time role lies entirely inside the full-time one, so the union is Jan 2020 to Dec 2022, 36 months. Summing gives 48 months only because 2021 is counted twice.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Let the LLM parse and let code do the date math
question: Why does `date(2023, 1, 31) + relativedelta(months=1)` return 2023-02-28 instead of raising an error or returning March 3?
options: relativedelta clamps to the last valid day: adding months never crosses a month boundary
It adds 28 days
It converts the date to a timestamp and adds 30 days
February 29 is skipped in non-leap years by adding 29 days
explain: The dateutil docs state that adding a month never crosses the month boundary, so day 31 is clamped to the last day of February. That is the calendar-month semantics you want for *Sep 2021 plus 3 years* style questions.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Search against a PRM, revisions, and compute-optimal allocation
question: A product mostly receives easy prompts that the model already solves 70% of the time. Which allocation does the paper's evidence favor?
options: Deep lookahead search against a PRM
Spend the budget sequentially (revise or keep reasoning) rather than on aggressive PRM search
Skip any verifier and return the first sample
Always use the maximum number of parallel samples
explain: On easy bins, sequential revisions did best and beam search degraded with budget. Light selection (vote or weighted best-of-N) over a revision chain is the safer choice.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: One gradient step on a key-value loss is the delta rule
question: Which pair of choices turns the generic TTT layer into plain linear attention?
options: Linear model, batch gradient descent, W_0 = 0
Linear model, online gradient descent, W_0 = 0
Two-layer MLP, batch gradient descent, learned W_0
Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression with a softmax kernel
explain: Theorem 1 of the TTT paper: linear model, batch GD (all gradients at W_0) and W_0 = 0 give linear attention. Online GD gives the delta rule instead. The kernel-regression option is Theorem 2, which recovers softmax attention, not linear attention. Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression predicts a weighted average of stored values, weighted by a kernel's similarity between the query and each stored key.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: One lock, many cores: why a shared slab cache stops scaling
question: Why did the original slab allocator get *slower* in total when going from 1 to 16 threads, rather than just staying flat?
options: Each thread ran its constructors twice
Contention made each lock handoff more expensive (cache line transfers, waiting, wakeups), so the serialized work itself took longer
The Starfire had only one memory controller
The slab layer disabled interrupts
explain: A flat ceiling assumes the critical section costs the same under load. Under contention the lock and freelist lines move between CPUs on every acquisition and waiters spin or sleep, so each serialized operation gets slower. The paper calls this increasingly pathological lock contention.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Today: thread caches, per-CPU caches and restartable sequences
question: In TCMalloc's rseq push (free), the code writes the object pointer into the slot and then stores the incremented `current`. Why is it fine if the thread is preempted between those two stores?
options: Preemption is disabled during free
The slot write is atomic
Nothing is published until the store to current commits; a restarted sequence just overwrites the same slot
The kernel replays the first store for it
explain: Only the final store to `current` makes the new object visible. If the thread is interrupted after writing the slot but before committing, the sequence restarts, recomputes the slot from the current header and rewrites it. TCMalloc's rseq notes describe exactly this: preempted sequences overwrite the deallocated object until one commits.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: STRIDE: six ways things go wrong
question: A banking app has no record of who approved a transfer, so a staff member can deny approving a fraudulent one. Which property is missing?
options: Availability
Confidentiality
Non-repudiation
Authentication
explain: Being able to deny an action because nothing trustworthy records it is repudiation, the threat against non-repudiation. The staff member was authenticated; the problem is the missing evidence.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Design principles I: simple, closed by default, checked every time
question: A service checks a user's permissions at login and caches the answer for the whole 8-hour session. Which principle does this strain, and why?
options: Open design, because the cache is secret
Economy of mechanism, because caching adds code
Complete mediation, because revoked rights keep working until the cached result expires
Fail-safe defaults, because the cache starts empty
explain: The paper warns to examine remembered authority checks sceptically: if authority changes, the remembered result must be updated. A fired employee's permissions should not survive 8 hours.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Who do you trust? Thompson's compiler and SolarWinds
question: SolarWinds' Orion updates were validly signed. What did the signature actually guarantee?
options: That the code had been reviewed for backdoors
That the update was safe to install
That the file came from SolarWinds' signing process unmodified after signing, not that the build was clean
Nothing, because the certificate was stolen
explain: CISA's advisory says the backdoored DLL was signed by the legitimate SolarWinds certificate. Signing proves origin and integrity after signing; it cannot detect tampering that happened before the signature, during the build.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: Promotion: finding hot pages trapped in slow memory
question: After you lower numa_balancing_promote_rate_limit_MBps, what does the kernel do to the hot threshold over the next windows?
options: Raises it, so more pages qualify
Lowers it step by step, so only pages touched sooner after scanning qualify
Leaves it unchanged; the rate limit only drops excess promotions
Resets it to 1000 ms every window
explain: A lower limit shrinks ref_cand. If candidates exceed 110% of that, the threshold drops by 125 ms per window (to a floor of 125 ms), so the candidate stream shrinks to match the budget instead of being cut off at random.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Prophet, the M4 competition and foundation models
question: An ML team's global gradient-boosting model (one model trained across all series, built from many small decision trees, each fitted to the errors of the trees before it) beats ARIMA on a single holdout month, but loses to seasonal naive on average across 12 rolling origins. What should ship?
options: The ML model, because it won the most recent month
ARIMA, because it is a statistical model
Seasonal naive, or a combination tested the same way, because it is best across origins
Nothing, because the metrics disagree
explain: One month is one sample; the average over 12 origins is the stronger evidence. If a cheap baseline wins under rolling-origin evaluation, ship it, or test a combination of methods, which M4 found to be consistently strong.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Resumption and 0-RTT: faster, and replayable
question: Why can a server not tell a replayed 0-RTT flight from the original by looking at it?
options: The attacker re-encrypts it with a new key
Early data is sent without encryption
The flight depends only on the PSK and the client's values; the server has not yet contributed fresh randomness, so a copy is byte-identical and decrypts correctly
Because the ticket has expired
explain: In a full handshake, the server's random and key share make every connection unique. Early data is sent before the server says anything, so nothing in it can be connection-specific from the server's side.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Chains and roots: how a browser validates a certificate
question: A server is configured to send only its leaf certificate, without the intermediate. Browsers on some laptops work, but a Python script fails with "unable to get local issuer certificate". Why?
options: Python does not support ECDSA certificates
The leaf certificate has expired
Python needs the root certificate to be sent by the server
Some browsers fetch or cache the missing intermediate (for example via the AIA URL); Python's ssl module does not, so it cannot build a path to a root
explain: Path building needs every link. Browsers often paper over a missing intermediate, which hides the misconfiguration. Fix the server to send the full chain (leaf plus intermediates).

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Certificate Transparency: logging every certificate
question: A rogue certificate for your domain was issued by a trusted CA but never logged to CT. What happens when an attacker uses it against a current Chrome user?
options: It works, because the CA signature is valid
Chrome shows it with a warning the user can click through
Chrome rejects it because it lacks the required SCTs
It works only on HTTP/1.1
explain: In CT-enforcing Chrome, publicly trusted certificates without enough valid SCTs fail validation. To be accepted the certificate has to be logged, which makes it visible to the domain owner.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Heartbleed: trusting a length field in OpenSSL
question: What single missing check caused Heartbleed?
options: A check that the peer's certificate was valid
A check that the payload length claimed in the heartbeat message was no larger than the data actually received
A check on the heartbeat message type
A check that encryption was enabled
explain: The code trusted an attacker-supplied length and copied that many bytes. Every length field from the network must be checked against the real buffer size before use.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Your first kernel: program_id, offsets and masks
question: Which version of the store line is a bug when N is not a multiple of BLOCK_SIZE?
options: tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, x + y, mask=mask)
tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, x + y, mask=offsets < n_elements)
tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, x + y)
None of them; tl.store never writes out of bounds
explain: Without a mask the last program writes all BLOCK_SIZE lanes, including addresses past the end of the output buffer. That corrupts neighboring memory or faults. The first two are the same mask written two ways.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Why one transformer should both read and draw images
question: A tokenizer downsamples by 16 in each direction. How many image positions does a 512 x 512 image take, not counting BOI and EOI?
explain: 512 / 16 = 32 per side, and 32 x 32 = 1024. This matches Chameleon, whose tokenizer turns a 512 x 512 image into 1024 tokens. 32 is only one side; 4096 is what an f = 8 tokenizer gives.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: One encoder or two: why Janus splits seeing from drawing
question: In the Janus ablation, replacing the shared VQ tokenizer with decoupled SigLIP + VQ raised MMBench from 35.0 to 69.4 while FID moved from 8.72 to 8.53. What does that suggest?
options: Generation quality was the bottleneck
The transformer was too small
A reconstruction-oriented tokenizer gives poor semantic features for understanding, and a dedicated understanding encoder fixes that without hurting generation
MMBench rewards image resolution only
explain: Generation was about the same in both rows, so the gain is almost all understanding. VQ codes are trained to rebuild pixels, not to expose meaning; SigLIP is trained to align images with text.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Booting on the hypervisor: virtual devices, boot time and memory
question: Mirage seals a unikernel so no page table changes are allowed after start of day. Which consequence must the application live with?
options: It cannot receive network packets
It must pre-allocate all the memory it needs at startup, since the heap cannot grow by mapping new pages
It cannot use a garbage collector
It must run with a single vCPU
explain: The paper states a sealed VM cannot expand its heap and must pre-allocate its memory at boot; allocation within the heap and I/O mappings still work. The single vCPU in Mirage is a separate design choice, not a consequence of sealing.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Graph traversal: memory layout, cache misses and prefetching
question: hnswlib prefetches `vector_of(data[j + 1])`. For a 768-d fp32 vector, what does that one instruction bring toward the cache?
options: All 3,212 bytes of the next neighbor's block
One 64-byte cache line at the start of the next neighbor's vector
The whole neighbor list of the next neighbor
Nothing on ARM builds without SSE, and everything on x86
explain: A prefetch hint covers the cache line containing the address. Here that is the first line of the vector. The remaining lines rely on the hardware stream prefetcher once the distance loop starts reading.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: One GRPO step through RayPPOTrainer, call by call
question: data.train_batch_size=512, rollout.n=8, actor.ppo_mini_batch_size=128, ppo_epochs=1. How many actor optimizer steps happen per RL step?
explain: 512 prompts x 8 = 4096 responses. The mini-batch is 128 prompts, which the trainer scales to 128 x 8 = 1024 responses. 4096 / 1024 = 4 optimizer steps. Reading ppo_mini_batch_size as responses would give 32, the common mistake.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Which frames to look at: uniform sampling and the needle problem
question: You must answer questions about 2-second events in 30-minute videos and can afford 256 frames. Which statement is right?
options: Uniform sampling hits about 28% of such events, so dense or question-aware selection is needed
Uniform sampling hits every event because 256 frames is a lot
Random sampling would hit more events than a uniform grid
Hit rate does not depend on video length
explain: $P = \min(1, 2 \times 256 / 1800) \approx 0.284$. A grid always does at least as well as independent random times for the same N, and the hit rate falls as the video gets longer.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Bigger context or captions: LongVA, Gemini 1.5, retrieval, benchmarks
question: A model scores 100% on a video needle-in-a-haystack test at 1 hour. What can you conclude?
options: It will answer any question about hour-long videos correctly
It can locate a single salient item anywhere in an hour of context; multi-event reasoning still needs benchmarks like Video-MME or LongVideoBench
Its frame sampling is uniform
It uses a memory bank
explain: A needle test isolates retrieval of one planted item. Real questions require combining several moments, ordering and counting, which is what the long splits of Video-MME and LongVideoBench's referring reasoning test.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: The dynamics model: next-frame tokens with MaskGIT
question: Generating 16 frames from one prompt frame with 25 MaskGIT steps per frame needs how many dynamics forward passes?
explain: The prompt frame is given, so 15 new frames are generated, each needing 25 passes: 15 x 25 = 375. This sequential cost is a big reason the original Genie ran near 1 FPS.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: A new head and a higher resolution
question: Why does DeiT resize position embeddings with bicubic rather than bilinear interpolation?
options: Bicubic is faster on GPUs
Bilinear interpolation shrinks the vectors' norm, and short embeddings hurt the pretrained network
Bilinear cannot resize a 14x14 grid to 24x24 because 24 is not a multiple of 14
Bicubic interpolates the CLS embedding too, which bilinear cannot
explain: DeiT's stated reason is the norm: averaging neighbors shortens vectors, and those low-norm embeddings are out of distribution for the pretrained blocks. Both methods handle any target size, and the CLS embedding is not interpolated at all; it is kept as is.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: Binning: one 7-DoF action becomes seven tokens
question: A dimension has bounds [-0.05, 0.05] m and 256 uniform bins. For an action inside the bounds, what is the largest possible decoding error?
options: 0.39 mm, one full bin
0.195 mm, half a bin
0.05 m, half the range
Zero, because the token stores the exact value
explain: The bin width is 0.1 m / 256 = 0.39 mm. Decoding returns the bin center, so the worst case is a value at a bin edge: half a bin, 0.195 mm.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: Running action chunks in the control loop
question: A Diffusion Policy user raises the execution horizon from 8 to 64 steps on a task where objects get bumped. Success drops. Why?
options: Longer chunks are less smooth
The diffusion model cannot predict more than 16 steps
Longer execution horizons increase the number of denoising steps per action
The robot executes many actions without looking, so it reacts slowly when the scene changes
explain: Executing more steps open-loop improves consistency but delays the next observation. Diffusion Policy's ablation found too long a horizon hurts because of slow reaction time, with 8 steps best for most tasks.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: VQGAN: perceptual and adversarial losses for 256-token images
question: Why did the VQGAN paper target 256 tokens per image rather than, say, 1024?
options: The codebook had only 256 entries
256 was the longest sequence they could feasibly train a 307M GPT-2 medium on with a 12 GB GPU
The perceptual loss only works on 16 x 16 grids
Longer sequences always give worse reconstructions
explain: The paper states 16 x 16 was the maximum feasible length for GPT-2 medium on a 12 GB GPU. The perceptual and adversarial losses were what made reconstructions at that strong compression good enough.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: How vLLM chooses a backend: priority lists and validation
